title: 第十九章入局第四章陆判第二十章寻刀
lines: 第十九章入局
天亮了。宋焘站在城门口，回头看了一眼那座破败的城隍庙。以前，他觉得那是他的家。现在，他觉得那是他的牢笼。
他摸了摸怀里，天书已经不在了。但他知道，那些字都在他心里，一个个，像烧红的烙铁。商三官，王半城，还有无数个还没名字的人。他深吸了一口气，空气里夹杂着尘土和早点铺子的油烟味。这是人间的味道，活人的味道。
“走吧。”他对自己说。
他没带判官笔，也没带官印。他只带了一身骨头，和一双看透了因果的眼睛。他要去看看，这人间，到底还有多少个王半城。
宋焘走了三天，走到河南府。他不知道自己为什么要来这里，只是觉得，该来了。
河南府很大，比他想的大得多。街上人来人往，有做买卖的，有拉车的，有挑担的，有抱着孩子讨饭的。他站在街边，看着这些人，心里忽然空了一块。他看了那么多因果，见了那么多生死，但他从来没有站在人群里过。他只是在书外看，像看一场戏。现在戏台拆了，他站在台上，不知道该怎么演。
他在街上站了一个时辰，没有人看他。他穿的是城隍的官服，但在人间，那就是一件旧袍子。他饿了。摸了摸口袋，一文钱也没有。他站在包子铺前，看着热腾腾的包子，咽了咽口水。包子铺的老板娘看了他一眼，说：“要买就买，不买别挡道。”他退到一边，站在墙根底下，看着街上的人来人往。
他忽然觉得，自己什么都不是。在天书前，他是城隍，管一方生死。在人间，他只是一个没钱的过路人，连一个包子都买不起。他蹲下来，抱着膝盖，看着地上的蚂蚁。蚂蚁在搬一粒米，搬不动，又来了几只，一起搬，还是搬不动。他伸出手，想帮它们。手指刚碰到米粒，蚂蚁全跑了。他缩回手，看着那粒米，看了很久。
“你蹲在这里做什么？”一个声音从头顶传来。
他抬起头，看见一个老头。老头穿着破旧的衣裳，脸上全是皱纹，手里拿着一根竹竿，竹竿上挂着一串铜钱。老头看着他，笑了。那笑很丑，牙掉了好几颗，但眼睛很亮，像两颗浸在溪水里的黑石子。
“饿了吧？”老头问。
宋焘点点头。老头从竹竿上取下几文钱，递给他。“去买两个包子。别饿着。”
宋焘接过钱，手在发抖。他站起来，走到包子铺前，买了两个包子。他递给老板娘一文钱，老板娘接过钱，看了他一眼，又看了老头一眼，叹了口气，又多给了他一个包子。
他捧着包子，走回墙根。老头还站在那里，看着他。
“吃吧。”老头说。
宋焘咬了一口包子，烫得他直吸气。老头笑了，蹲下来，和他并排坐着。
“你是外地来的？”老头问。
“来做什么？”
宋焘想了想。“找人。”
“找谁？”
“找王半城。”
老头愣了一下，然后笑了。“王半城？那是十几年前的事了。王半城早死了。”
宋焘的手停了。包子还在手里，热腾腾的。“怎么死的？”
“被人杀了。”老头说，“一个女子，替她爹报仇。杀了王半城，自己也死了。那女子是个烈女，官府给她立了碑。你要找王半城，找不到了。你要找那女子的碑，出城往南走，三里地，路边有一座坟，那就是。”
宋焘没有说话。他低下头，看着手里的包子。包子已经凉了，油渗出来，沾在他手指上。
content_en:
Chapter 19 Entering the Game
It's dawn. Song Tao stood at the city gate and looked back at the dilapidated City God's Temple. Before, he felt it was his home. Now, he felt like it was his prison.
He touched his arms and found that the Book of Heaven was no longer there. But he knew that those words were all in his heart, one by one, like a red-hot iron. Shang Sanguan, Wang Bancheng, and countless others who have yet to be named. He took a deep breath. The air was filled with the smell of dust and the fumes from the earlier store. This is the taste of the human world, the taste of a living person.
"Let's go," he said to himself.
He didn't bring the judge's pen or official seal. He only had a body of bones and a pair of eyes that could see through cause and effect. He wanted to see how many kings and half cities there were in this world.
Song Tao walked for three days and reached Henan Mansion. He didn't know why he came here, he just felt that it was time to come.
Henan Mansion is huge, much bigger than he thought. People were coming and going on the street, including people doing business, pulling carts, carrying burdens, and begging for food with their children in their arms. He stood on the street, looking at these people, and suddenly felt an emptiness in his heart. He has seen so much cause and effect, and seen so much life and death, but he has never stood in a crowd. He just watched it outside the book, like watching a play. Now that the stage has been dismantled, he is standing on the stage, not knowing how to act.
He stood in the street for an hour, no one looked at him. He was wearing the official uniform of the City God, but in the human world, it was just an old robe. He is hungry. I touched my pocket, but there was not a penny. He stood in front of the bun shop, looked at the hot buns, and swallowed. The proprietress of the bun shop glanced at him and said, "If you want to buy, buy it. If you don't want to buy, don't block the way." He stepped aside and stood under the wall, watching the people coming and going on the street.
He suddenly felt that he was nothing. In front of the Book of Heaven, he is the city god, in charge of life and death. In the human world, he is just a passerby without money, who cannot even afford a bun. He squatted down, hugged his knees, and looked at the ants on the ground. The ants were moving a grain of rice, but they couldn't move it. Then a few more ants came and moved them together, but they still couldn't move it. He reached out his hand to help them. As soon as my fingers touched the rice grains, all the ants ran away. He retracted his hand and looked at the grain of rice for a long time.
"What are you doing squatting here?" A voice came from above.
He raised his head and saw an old man. The old man was wearing shabby clothes, his face was full of wrinkles, and he was holding a bamboo pole with a bunch of copper coins hanging on it. The old man looked at him and smiled. The smile was ugly, with several teeth missing, but the eyes were bright, like two black pebbles soaked in the stream.
"Are you hungry?" the old man asked.
Song Tao nodded. The old man took a few pennies from the bamboo pole and handed them to him. "Go buy two buns. Don't go hungry."
Song Tao took the money, his hands shaking. He stood up, walked to the bun shop and bought two buns. He handed the proprietress a penny. The proprietress took the money, looked at him, then looked at the old man, sighed, and gave him another bun.
He held the bun and walked back to the wall. The old man was still standing there, looking at him.
"Eat." said the old man.
Song Tao took a bite of the bun, which was so hot that he took a breath. The old man smiled, squatted down, and sat side by side with him.
"Are you from out of town?" the old man asked.
"Yes."
"What are you doing here?"
Song Tao thought for a while. "Find someone."
"Who are you looking for?"
"Looking for Wang Bancheng."
The old man was stunned for a moment, then smiled. "Wang Bancheng? That was more than ten years ago. Wang Bancheng died long ago."
Song Tao's hand stopped. The bun is still in my hand, still hot. "How did you die?"
"She was killed." The old man said, "A woman avenged her father. She killed Wang Bancheng and died herself. The woman was a martyr, and the government set up a monument for her. You are looking for Wang Bancheng, but you can't find it. If you are looking for the woman's monument, go south out of the city. There is a tomb on the roadside three miles away, that's it."
Song Tao said nothing. He lowered his head and looked at the bun in his hand. The buns had cooled down, and the oil seeped out and stuck to his fingers.
